summary: Describes conventions for using several cryptographic algorithms with the EncryptedPrivateKeyInfo structure from RFC 5958, and for protecting the AsymmetricKeyPackage content type with various Cryptographic Message Syntax types. It is a Proposed Standard.

plainLanguage.summary: A private key has to be stored and moved somewhere, and it must be protected on the way. RFC 5958 defined two containers for it but left the choice of algorithms open. This document closes that gap: it says which algorithms to use for each way of protecting a key package, so that two implementations do the same thing.

questions: how to encrypt a private key with a password
which algorithms protect asymmetric key packages
what is aes key wrap with padding
subtitle: Which cryptographic algorithms to use when protecting private keys and key packages with CMS.

tldr.problem: Private keys and key packages need protecting, but RFC 5958 leaves open which algorithms an implementation should use for that.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 5959 picks existing algorithms: password-based encryption with PBES2 for EncryptedPrivateKeyInfo, and per-type MUST and SHOULD lists for the five CMS types that can wrap an AsymmetricKeyPackage. It defines no new algorithms.
tldr.outcome: Implementations of CMS-protected key packages are recommended to follow these conventions. The RFC is a Proposed Standard and was later updated by RFC 6162.

facts.label: Required PBE scheme
facts.value: PBES2 with PBKDF2 using HMAC with SHA-256

today: RFC 5959 is a Proposed Standard published in August 2010. It has not been obsoleted, but it was updated by RFC 6162.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content:
This document describes the conventions for using several cryptographic algorithms with the EncryptedPrivateKeyInfo structure defined in RFC 5958. The EncryptedPrivateKeyInfo is used by PKCS #12 to encrypt a PrivateKeyInfo. It is similar to EncryptedData in that it has no recipients, no originators and no content encryption keys, and requires keys to be managed by other means.

The document also includes conventions necessary to protect the AsymmetricKeyPackage content type with the Cryptographic Message Syntax protecting content types: SignedData, EnvelopedData, EncryptedData, AuthenticatedData and AuthEnvelopedData. Implementations of AsymmetricKeyPackage do not require support for any CMS protecting content type; however, if the AsymmetricKeyPackage is CMS protected it is RECOMMENDED that the conventions defined here be followed.

The document does not define any new algorithms; it refers to previously defined ones.
sections.plainLanguage: A private key has to be stored and moved somewhere, and it must be protected on the way. RFC 5958 defined two containers for it but left the choice of algorithms open. This document closes that gap: it says which algorithms to use for each way of protecting a key package, so that two implementations do the same thing.

sections.title: EncryptedPrivateKeyInfo
sections.content:
The de facto standard used to encrypt the PrivateKeyInfo structure, which is subsequently placed in the EncryptedPrivateKeyInfo encryptedData field, is Password Based Encryption based on PKCS #5 and PKCS #12. The major difference between PKCS #5 and PKCS #12 is the supported encoding for the password: ASCII for PKCS #5 and Unicode for PKCS #12. PKCS #5 specifies two PBE schemes, PBES 1 and 2, and recommends PBES2 for new specifications.

PBES2 with a key derivation algorithm of PBKDF2 using HMAC with SHA-256 and an encryption algorithm of AES Key Wrap with Padding MUST be supported. AES-256 Key Wrap with Padding MAY also be supported as an encryption algorithm.
sections.plainLanguage: The usual way to protect a private key with a password runs through PBES2. The password is turned into a key with PBKDF2 using HMAC with SHA-256, and that key wraps the private key with AES Key Wrap with Padding. Every implementation must support that combination.

sections.title: SignedData
sections.content: CMS can be used to protect the AsymmetricKeyPackage, and this document gives guidance for each of the five protecting content types. If an implementation supports SignedData, then it MUST support the signature scheme RSA and SHOULD support the signature schemes RSASSA-PSS and DSA. Implementations MUST support, in concert with these signature schemes, the hash function SHA-256, and SHOULD support the hash function SHA-1.
sections.plainLanguage: SignedData adds a signature to the package. An implementation that supports it must be able to sign with RSA and hash with SHA-256; RSASSA-PSS, DSA and SHA-1 are recommended as well.

sections.title: EnvelopedData
sections.content:
If an implementation supports EnvelopedData, then it MUST implement key transport and it MAY implement key agreement. When key transport is used, RSA encryption MUST be supported and RSAES-OAEP SHOULD be supported. When key agreement is used, Diffie-Hellman ephemeral-static MUST be supported.

Since the content type is used to carry a cryptographic key and its attributes, an algorithm that is traditionally used to encrypt one key with another is employed. Regardless of the key management technique chosen, implementations MUST support AES-128 Key Wrap with Padding as the content encryption algorithm, and SHOULD support AES-256 Key Wrap with Padding.

When key agreement is used, a key wrap algorithm is also specified to wrap the content encryption key. If the content encryption algorithm is AES-128 Key Wrap with Padding, then the key wrap algorithm MUST be AES-128 Key Wrap with Padding. If the content encryption algorithm is AES-256 Key Wrap with Padding, then the key wrap algorithm MUST be AES-256 Key Wrap with Padding.
sections.plainLanguage: EnvelopedData encrypts the package for one or more recipients. RSA key transport is required and Diffie-Hellman key agreement may be added. Whatever way the content key is shared, the package itself is encrypted with AES-128 Key Wrap with Padding, and the 256-bit version is recommended. When key agreement is used, the content key is wrapped with the same algorithm that encrypts the package.

sections.title: EncryptedData, AuthenticatedData and AuthEnvelopedData
sections.content:
If an implementation supports EncryptedData, then it MUST implement AES-128 Key Wrap with Padding and SHOULD implement AES-256 Key Wrap with Padding. EncryptedData requires that keys be managed by other means, so the only algorithm specified is the content encryption algorithm, and since the content type carries a cryptographic key and its attributes, an algorithm traditionally used to encrypt one key with another is employed.

If an implementation supports AuthenticatedData, then it MUST implement SHA-256 as the message digest algorithm and SHOULD support SHA-1. HMAC with SHA-256 MUST be supported, and HMAC with SHA-1 SHOULD be supported.

If an implementation supports AuthEnvelopedData, then it MUST implement the EnvelopedData recommendations except for the content encryption algorithm, which in this case MUST be AES-GCM; the 128-bit version MUST be implemented and the 256-bit version SHOULD be implemented. Implementations MAY also support AES-CCM.
sections.plainLanguage: The remaining three CMS types have simpler rules. EncryptedData encrypts the package with a key managed elsewhere, so only AES-128 Key Wrap with Padding is required. AuthenticatedData adds a message authentication code, and requires SHA-256 and HMAC with SHA-256. AuthEnvelopedData does both at once, using AES-GCM with 128-bit keys.

sections.title: Public Key Sizes
sections.content: The easiest way to implement the SignedData, EnvelopedData and AuthEnvelopedData content types is with public key certificates. If an implementation supports RSA, RSASSA-PSS, DSS, RSAES-OAEP or DH, then it MUST support key lengths from 1024-bit to 2048-bit, inclusive.
sections.plainLanguage: Whichever public key algorithm an implementation uses, it has to handle key lengths from 1024 to 2048 bits, inclusive.

sections.title: The SMIMECapabilities Attribute
sections.content: The SMIMECapabilities attribute is defined as a mechanism for recipients to indicate their supported capabilities, including the algorithms they support. This document gives the attribute values for AES Key Wrap with Padding when used as a content encryption algorithm: AES-128 KW with Padding is 30 0d 06 09 60 86 48 01 65 03 04 01 08, AES-192 KW with Padding is 30 0d 06 09 60 86 48 01 65 03 04 01 1C, and AES-256 KW with Padding is 30 0d 06 09 60 86 48 01 65 03 04 01 30.
sections.plainLanguage: The S/MIME capability attribute is how a recipient says which algorithms it can handle. The document gives the exact byte values to use for the three AES key wrap sizes.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The security considerations from the documents behind each of the algorithms apply. The strength of any encryption scheme is only as good as its weakest link, which in the case of a PBES is the password. Passwords need to provide sufficient entropy to ensure they cannot be easily guessed.

The NIST Electronic Authentication Guidance indicates that a user-chosen 20-character password from a 94-character keyboard with no checks provides 36 bits of entropy. If the 20-character password is randomly chosen, the amount of entropy is increased to roughly 131 bits. The amount of entropy in the password does not correlate directly to bits of security, but in general the more the better.

The choice of content encryption algorithms for this document was based on the reasoning that in the design of some high assurance cryptographic modules it is desirable to segregate cryptographic keying material from other data, and that the use of a specific cryptographic mechanism solely for the protection of cryptographic keying material can assist in this goal. Unfortunately, there is no AES-GCM or AES-CCM mode that provides the same properties. If such a mode is defined, the document will be updated to adopt that algorithm. The NIST key management guidance provides comparable bits of security for some algorithms and key sizes, and also provides time frames during which certain numbers of bits of security are appropriate, which some environments may find useful.
sections.plainLanguage: The weakest link in password-based protection is the password itself. The RFC quotes the NIST guidance: a 20-character password that a person chose gives about 36 bits of entropy, and the same length chosen at random gives about 131. It also explains why key wrap was chosen over AES-GCM and AES-CCM for the content encryption: key wrap keeps keying material separate from other data, and the authenticated modes do not provide those same properties.

items.text: The password-based encryption scheme that turns a password into an encryption key.

items.text: The key derivation function, which makes each guess of the password more expensive.

items.text: The algorithm that encrypts the private key once the key is derived.

items.text: The weakest link, so it needs enough entropy to resist guessing.
